clue.text: Frenchman at the races may have luck with this

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for Monsieur, the French title for a man
Ascot is the famous racecourse in Berkshire, England, home of Royal Ascot

explanation.surface: A Frenchman going to the horse races hopes for a bit of luck.
explanation.walkthrough: ASCOT is a racecourse in Berkshire, England, where Royal Ascot is held. The definition is loose: a charm carried for luck.
explanation.definitionFit: A mascot is a charm or figure kept to bring good fortune to its owner.

clue.text: City three thousand miles across?

parts.note: reads as a vast city, but names an ocean whose name also goes before City in a New Jersey resort, and which is about that wide

explanation.surface: Imagine a city three thousand miles wide.
explanation.walkthrough: Atlantic City is a New Jersey resort; the ocean of the same name is roughly three thousand miles wide.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocean between Europe and America is some three thousand miles across and lends its name to a New Jersey resort city.

clue.text: Not an original claim to land tenure

parts.note: a copy is a reproduction, not the original
a hold is a grip or claim on something

explanation.surface: A claim to own land that is not genuine.
explanation.walkthrough: Copyhold was an old English form of tenure recorded on the manor's court roll, of which the tenant held a copy.
explanation.definitionFit: Copyhold was a historic English form of holding land, proved by a copy of the manorial roll.

clue.text: Sound sleeper to obstruct arrangement of sheets

parts.note: a spinning top is said to sleep when it spins so steadily it seems still, hence sleep like a top
to hamper is to obstruct

explanation.surface: A heavy sleeper gets in the way of making the bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sheets' suggests bedding, but on a sailing ship sheets are ropes; top hamper is the upper rigging and sails.
explanation.definitionFit: Top hamper is a ship's upper masts, sails and rigging, where the ropes controlling sails are arranged.

clue.text: Capital restraint of top players

parts.note: the head is the top of the body
a band is a group of musicians playing together

explanation.surface: A tight rein is kept on the leading performers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' here means 'of the head' (Latin caput), not a city: a band that restrains the hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A headband is a strip worn round the forehead to hold the hair in place.

clue.text: Confuse fasts with the revival of Christian observance

indicators.note: to confuse letters is to mix them up into a new order

explanation.surface: Fasting gets mixed up with a religious revival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confuse' shuffles FASTS and THE REVIVAL together; 'with' is the joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: A church thanksgiving held each autumn for the gathered crops.

clue.text: The spirit, of the dark and gloomy church?

parts.note: dun is a dull greyish-brown, a dark gloomy colour
kirk is the Scottish word for church

explanation.surface: Asks whether the spirit belongs to some dark and dismal church.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dunkirk spirit is the British phrase for courage in adversity, after the 1940 evacuation; KIRK is Scots for church.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase for pulling together in a crisis comes from the 1940 evacuation, so the town's name qualifies spirit.

clue.text: Agreement for examination on this

explanation.surface: Consent is given for an inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: Goods sent 'on approval' may be examined and returned if unwanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Consent or favourable opinion; and the trade phrase 'on approval' for goods sent to be inspected before purchase.

clue.text: Black state of Conrad's heart?

explanation.surface: Asks what lies at the black core of Joseph Conrad.
explanation.walkthrough: Joseph Conrad wrote the novella Heart of Darkness.
explanation.definitionFit: A condition with no light; and the word completing the title of Conrad's novella about the Congo.

clue.text: Knowing a set of questions that will trap pests

parts.note: fly is British slang for sharp or knowing
an examination paper is a set of questions

explanation.surface: A cunning quiz is designed to catch out troublesome students.
explanation.walkthrough: FLY is British slang for shrewd or knowing.
explanation.definitionFit: Flypaper is a sticky strip hung up so that insects land on it and are caught.

clue.text: Potential assassin makes bargain with monarch

parts.note: a snip is British slang for a bargain
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A would-be killer strikes a deal with a king.
explanation.walkthrough: A SNIP is British slang for a bargain; ER is the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A sniper shoots from hiding and is often the hidden gunman in a planned killing.

clue.text: Pound — one canto he just 'started

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: to pound something is to beat it to pieces, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Ezra Pound has only just begun another of his Cantos.
explanation.walkthrough: Ezra Pound wrote The Cantos, so 'Pound' looks like the poet; it is the anagram signal, shuffling I, CANTO and HE.
explanation.definitionFit: Inchoate means only begun, still in an undeveloped early stage.

clue.text: Popular complaint about dead language

indicators.note: the word for complaint goes around the word for popular

parts.note: a moan is a complaint
in means fashionable or popular

explanation.surface: People grumble generally about a language no one speaks any more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts MOAN around IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Minoan was the tongue of ancient Crete, now extinct and only partly deciphered.

clue.text: Spit out, and moisten either side with mouth preparation

indicators.note: the word for moisten sits on both sides of the jumbled letters

parts.note: to lick is to wet with the tongue

indicators.note: out signals the letters of spit are put out of order

explanation.surface: Someone spits, then wets their lips with their tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges SPIT to IPST, and 'either side' splits LICK around it: L, IPST, ICK.
explanation.definitionFit: Lipstick is a cosmetic applied to colour the lips.

clue.text: Singer's husky delivery on Scottish island!

parts.note: chaff is the husks separated from grain when it is threshed
inch is a Scottish word for a small island

explanation.surface: A vocalist's hoarse performance on a Scottish isle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' and 'husky' suggest a voice; the singer is a songbird and 'husky' means made of husks.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaffinch is a common songbird, a finch with a cheerful warbling call.

clue.text: Finished off the cake from the freezer?.

explanation.surface: Someone completes the cake by taking it out of the deep freeze.
explanation.definitionFit: A cake is finished by coating it in sugar topping; something straight from deep cold is frozen and chilled.

clue.text: Permitted to follow the Devil without question

indicators.note: to follow places the word for permitted after the little devil

parts.note: an imp is a little devil
licit means permitted or lawful

explanation.surface: Allowed to follow Satan without asking any questions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to follow' puts LICIT after IMP.
explanation.definitionFit: As in implicit trust: absolute and unquestioning.

clue.text: Honourably retired from working? Semi-true

indicators.note: working here means the letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: Asks whether someone honourably retired from work is only half right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'working' rearranges the letters of SEMI-TRUE; 'from work' is the obvious reading of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Emeritus describes a professor who keeps an honorary title after leaving office.

clue.text: A record, second highest in the European charts

parts.note: LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: A record reaches number two in the European hit parade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charts' looks like music charts but means maps, on which these mountains are Europe's highest.
explanation.definitionFit: This range holds western Europe's loftiest peaks, Mont Blanc among them.

clue.text: General resemblance to Humpty Dumpty?

explanation.surface: Asks what a general has in common with an egg-shaped nursery figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Humpty Dumpty, the nursery-rhyme egg, is round all over.
explanation.definitionFit: Comprehensive or versatile; and spherical in every direction, like an egg.

clue.text: Some subjects for Dip Ed: (i) Greek (ii) History

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: Lists two subjects studied for a diploma in education.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits inside DIP ED (I) GREEK, with the numeral i supplying a letter; 'History' looks like a subject but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedigree is a recorded line of descent, an ancestral record.

clue.text: A sudden come-down, having to wait for opening time!

definitions.text: A sudden come-down, having to wait for opening time!

parts.words: A sudden come-down, having to wait for opening time!
parts.note: reads like a drinker waiting for the pub to open, but describes a skydiver dropping until the parachute opens

explanation.surface: A thirsty drinker is let down, stuck waiting for the pub to open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening time' suggests British pub hours; it is the moment a parachute opens.
explanation.definitionFit: The stretch of a parachute jump before the canopy opens is a plunge without any check.

clue.text: Projection for strengthening a central political organisation

indicators.note: central means the letter is set inside the word for a projection

parts.note: a flange is a projecting rim that strengthens or attaches a part

explanation.surface: A support projecting from a central party structure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'central' puts A inside FLANGE. The Falange was the Spanish fascist party.
explanation.definitionFit: The Falange was Franco's Spanish fascist party.

clue.text: Proud of the butter-dish set before Sisera

definitions.text: of the butter-dish set before Sisera

explanation.surface: A haughty serving dish is set before a biblical general.
explanation.walkthrough: In Judges 5:25 Jael 'brought forth butter in a lordly dish' to Sisera before killing him.
explanation.definitionFit: Haughty, grand bearing; and the Bible's adjective for the noble dish Jael used to serve Sisera.

clue.text: It protects those easily tempted -. to 'move aft first

indicators.note: first places the shuffled letters ahead of the next piece
the letters of aft are moved into a new order

parts.note: the frail are those morally weak and easily led astray

explanation.surface: A safeguard for the weak-willed: shift to the back first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'move' rearranges AFT to TAF, and 'first' puts it before FRAIL. 'aft' hints at a ship, where this rail sits at the stern.
explanation.definitionFit: A taffrail is the guard rail round a ship's stern, keeping people from falling overboard.

clue.text: Site of 'miracle — note included in scriptural commentary

indicators.note: the musical note is included within the place name

parts.note: Cana in Galilee is where Jesus turned water into wine
te is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A gospel commentary includes a note on where a miracle happened.
explanation.walkthrough: CANA is where, in John's gospel, water was turned into wine; 'included' puts TE inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A catena is a chain of extracts from the Church Fathers, linked as a running gloss on a biblical text.

clue.text: Front vehicle needs protection

parts.note: a van is a road vehicle
a guard gives protection

explanation.surface: The leading vehicle requires an escort.
explanation.definitionFit: The vanguard is the foremost part of an advancing army or movement.

clue.text: Sample not quite complete that's not common.

parts.note: to taste is to sample

indicators.note: not quite means the word for complete loses its final letter

parts.note: full means complete

explanation.surface: A partial sample that is far from ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' drops the last L of FULL.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing refined judgement rather than vulgarity, the opposite of coarse.

clue.text: Worked in the fields, but got laid off

explanation.surface: A farmhand worked the land but was then made redundant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laid off' suggests losing a job; in betting, to lay off a bet is to offset it, protecting against loss.
explanation.definitionFit: Farm labour trimming and laying field boundaries of bushes; and offsetting a wager to cover a possible loss.
